objectives: Explain what a token is and why models see ids not text
Describe how embeddings map ids to vectors

slides.title: Part 1 — Why text must become numbers
slides.body: A neural network multiplies matrices of floats. It has never seen a letter. Everything starts here.

slides.title: The model never sees text
slides.body:
To a transformer, input is a tensor of integers, then of vectors. The pipeline is fixed:

`text → tokens → integer ids → embedding vectors`

A **tokenizer** chops the string into units (tokens) and maps each to an id in a fixed **vocabulary**. An **embedding table** (a learned `vocab × d` matrix) turns each id into a dense vector. The model only ever sees that last form.

slides.title: Why not feed characters or words directly?
slides.body:
Two naive options, both bad:

- **Characters:** vocabulary is tiny (~100) but sequences are *long* — "transformer" is 11 steps. Attention cost grows with sequence length, so this is slow and forces the model to relearn spelling.
- **Whole words:** sequences are short but the vocabulary is unbounded — every typo, name, and compound is a new token, and unseen words become `<unk>` (information destroyed).

**Subword** tokenization (next lesson: BPE) is the engineering compromise: frequent words stay whole, rare words split into reusable pieces, nothing is `<unk>`.

slides.title: The sequence-length tax
slides.body: Every token you emit costs compute *and* a slot in the context window. Self-attention is $O(n^2)$ in sequence length $n$. So a tokenizer that produces 30% more tokens for the same text makes the model ~1.7× more expensive on that text and eats context budget. Tokenization is a latency and cost decision, not just preprocessing.

slides.title: Ids are labels, not magnitudes
slides.body: Token id 5000 is not "twice" id 2500 — ids are arbitrary labels. That's exactly why we don't feed the id; we feed `embedding_table[id]`, a learned vector. Similar tokens end up with similar vectors *because training pushed them there*, not because their ids are close.

slides.title: Whitespace, case, and the leading space
slides.body: Modern tokenizers attach the leading space to the next token, so `" cat"` and `"cat"` are *different* tokens. Case matters too (`Cat` ≠ `cat`) unless the tokenizer lowercases. These invisible distinctions explain many "why did the prompt behave differently?" mysteries — a stray leading space changes the token sequence.

slides.title: Numbers and code tokenize badly
slides.body: BPE merges are learned from mostly-prose corpora, so `1234567` may split into odd chunks like `123`,`45`,`67`, and code punctuation fragments heavily. That's why early LLMs were poor at arithmetic and why code models use code-aware tokenizers — the *tokenization*, not the reasoning, was a big part of the failure.

question.question: A word-level tokenizer is trained, then deployed. A user types a brand-new product name it never saw. What happens?
options: It is mapped to a single special "unknown" token, losing all information in that name
The tokenizer invents a new vocabulary entry on the fly
The model reads it character by character automatically
question.explanation: A pure word tokenizer has a vocabulary fixed at training time. Anything unseen collapses to a single `<unk>` token — the model literally cannot tell one unknown word from another. This out-of-vocabulary failure is the core reason subword tokenization replaced word tokenization.

question.question: Tokenizer A averages 4 characters/token; tokenizer B averages 2 characters/token. For the same document, roughly how does B's self-attention compute compare to A's?
options: About 4× more (cost grows with the square of token count)
The same — attention cost doesn't depend on the tokenizer
About half (fewer characters per token is cheaper)
question.explanation: B produces 2× as many tokens for the same text (half the characters per token). Self-attention is O(n²) in the token count, so doubling n quadruples that term: (2n)² / n² = 4×. Token efficiency is a real architectural lever, not a cosmetic detail.

question.question: Order these from FEWEST to MOST tokens produced for the same 500-word English paragraph.
question.explanation: Word-level emits roughly one token per word (~500). Subword splits some rare words into 2–3 pieces, so it is a bit higher (~650). Character-level emits one token per character (~2,800). Fewer tokens means shorter sequences and cheaper attention — but word-level pays for it with the out-of-vocabulary problem, which is why subword wins in practice.

slides.title: From text to model input, precisely
slides.body: Tokenization is a deterministic function `str → int[]`; embedding is a lookup `int[] → float[n][d]`. The vocabulary and the embedding table are *learned artifacts* shipped with the model — change the tokenizer and every id (and the embedding table) is invalidated. Derive the pipeline:

question.question: From text to model input
question.goal: Reconstruct how raw text becomes something a network can consume.

steps.prompt: A net needs fixed numeric input. First step from raw text?
steps.motivation: Models operate on integer ids over a fixed vocabulary, not characters.

options: Split into tokens, map each to an integer id
Feed raw UTF-8 bytes as floats
Hash the whole string to one number

hints: The vocabulary is finite and fixed.
steps.reveal: Tokenize → map each token to an id in a fixed vocab.

steps.prompt: Why embed ids into vectors instead of using the integer id directly?
steps.motivation: An id is a label, not a magnitude — arithmetic on it is meaningless; a learned vector captures similarity.

rubricCriteria.description: an integer id has no meaningful order or magnitude
embeddings are learnable dense vectors capturing similarity
the embedding table is trained jointly with the model

steps.reveal: Ids index a learned embedding table; the vectors — not the ids — carry meaning.

question.finalResult: text → tokens → ids → learned embedding vectors

slides.title: The classic tokenization failure
slides.body: A model looks "broken" on emoji, rare Unicode, or a new domain — usually it's the *tokenizer*, not the weights: out-of-distribution characters shatter into many low-signal tokens the model never trained on. Diagnose:

question.question: Diagnose the tokenization failure.
question.scenario: A model trained on English text suddenly performs terribly on user input full of emoji and rare Unicode symbols. The tokenizer and vocabulary are unchanged.

rubricCriteria.description: rare/unseen characters fragment into many subword or byte fallback tokens
the sequence balloons / meaning is diluted across many tokens
fix: broaden tokenizer coverage (e.g. byte-level BPE) or retrain the vocab

question.explanation: Out-of-distribution characters have no merged tokens, so they shatter into many tiny tokens — long, low-signal sequences the model never trained on.

hints: What corpus was the BPE vocab trained on?
Rare/unseen substrings have no merged token.
slides.workedSolution: BPE's merges come from frequent pairs in training text (mostly prose). Code symbols are rare there, so they remain unmerged subwords — more tokens for the same word count.

question.question: A 10-word English sentence becomes ~12 tokens, but a 10-word code snippet becomes ~40. Why?
options: Code has many rare substrings the BPE vocab never merged, so it fragments into more subword tokens
The model is simply larger for code
Code uses more characters per word, nothing else
question.explanation: BPE merges frequent pairs from its (mostly prose) training corpus; code identifiers/punctuation are comparatively rare, so they stay split into many short tokens.

question.prompt: Explain to your pet how text becomes model input.

rubricCriteria.description: tokens are the discrete units the model sees
embeddings are learned, not arbitrary numbers

slides.title: What to carry forward
slides.body: Tokens are the atoms everything else is built on. Next: **[BPE](/paths/ml-engineer/lessons/bpe-tokenization)** — the exact algorithm that *builds* the vocabulary you just relied on, and the vocab-size ↔ sequence-length tradeoff in numbers.
